overview: This file documents Japanese censorship of international commercial cable and radio traffic in Japanese-occupied Chinese treaty ports during the first half of 1938. Cross-reference sheets and two diplomatic telegrams report requirements to disclose commercial codes or supply codebooks at Tianjin, Shanghai, and Yantai, together with protests or objections by American, British, and German interests. The correspondence emphasizes the threatened delay, exposure of confidential business information, and possible economic harm caused by censorship, while also recording attempts to preserve procedures previously used under Chinese administration.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Oppenheimer Casing Company letter on censorship at Tientsin
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a letter protesting Japanese censorship of cables and radio messages sent from Tientsin to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The referenced letter concerned Japanese inspection of communications before their dispatch from Tientsin to the United States. The company feared that censorship would directly harm its business importing sausage casings.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Gauss telegram on coded commercial messages at Shanghai
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to telegram no. 164 concerning Japanese censorship of coded commercial messages at Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Japanese authorities announced that coded commercial messages passing through Shanghai cable offices would be censored. Gauss reported efforts to devise a practical solution, with the chief censor apparently agreeing to continue procedures formerly followed under Chinese censorship.

subfiles.title: Gauss telegram on Japanese censorship of Shanghai commercial cables
subfiles.about: Gauss objects to Japanese censorship of American commercial code messages and describes a proposed accommodation based on earlier Chinese procedures.
subfiles.summary: Japanese authorities announced that commercial code messages passing through Shanghai cable offices would be subject to censorship, potentially delaying traffic and exposing both message contents and proprietary codes. Gauss told the Japanese Consul General that he could not recognize a Japanese right to censor the coded messages of American firms and nationals, citing Japan's earlier refusal to accept Chinese censorship of Japanese-language cable traffic to Japan. Pending a settlement, the chief censor and cable companies appeared prepared to accept messages bearing a foreign consular seal or covered by a consular undertaking that they contained no military or national information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Roberts telegram on codebook demands at Chefoo
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram reporting that Japanese authorities required Chefoo firms to supply codebooks before coded messages would be delivered.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram reported Japanese demands that local firms present their codebooks so incoming coded messages could be decoded before delivery. British and German firms were protesting, while no American firm had yet registered a complaint.

subfiles.title: Roberts telegram on Japanese codebook requirements at Chefoo
subfiles.about: Roberts reports Japanese requirements for decoding incoming private-code messages at Chefoo and the response of foreign firms.
subfiles.summary: Beginning June 13, Japanese authorities required local firms to present codebooks so that incoming coded messages could be decoded before delivery. German and British interests protested the measure. No American firm had yet received a message in private code, and no complaint had been lodged with the U.S. Consulate.

interest: The file provides a compact view of how military occupation translated into control over routine commercial communications in Chinese treaty ports. Especially useful is Gauss's argument based on Japanese resistance to earlier Chinese censorship, together with the practical compromise involving consular seals and assurances. The contrast between Shanghai's negotiated procedure and Chefoo's demand for firms' codebooks illustrates local variation in censorship practice and shows how diplomatic objections often arose before American businesses had suffered a documented incident.
